Developing with Purpose:
How AI Changed Product Development, Not Just Coding

October 2026

(0:30) Hi everyone, and thanks for coming. This talk is called Developing with Purpose: how AI changed product development, not just coding. Most of what we hear about AI is about writing code faster. That's real, but it's not the biggest change. In the next fifteen minutes I'll show you why, what we do instead at Deriv, which we call X-Factory, and then we'll go to the workshop and build something live. Next: "Let's start with something we all know."

X-Factory — Why change

02 / 18

(0:45) Coding is no longer the bottleneck. An AI agent can write most of the code for a feature in minutes. So you'd expect every team to be shipping many times faster. Most teams aren't. Why? Because typing the code was never the hard part. The hard part is deciding what to build, reviewing what was built, and proving that it works. And those steps still run at human speed. Next: "Here's what that looks like on a timeline."

X-Factory — Why change

04 / 18

(1:15) AI agents already run many parts of Deriv. Here are a few of them. Small bugs get fixed straight from Slack: someone triggers an agent and it fixes the bug. Forge and Lexi are two of our bug-fix agents. QA, security and PII agents check our work, every pull request is reviewed by our AI review workflow in GitHub, our AI Release Manager deploys to production, and our AI Maintenance Agent handles issues once apps are live. Others look after system owners, payments, hiring, HR communication and customer experience, and major operational processes, like access requests, are automated end to end. And there are many more. So agents aren't the new part: review, release and maintenance are already AI-native. The gap is at the start: going from an idea to production-ready code. Next: "And that's where building with AI looks cheaper than it is."

05 / 18

(1:00) Building with AI looks cheap. It isn't. On the left is what we tend to assume. A prototype is one prompt away. Changing it in code is quick. And the demo is almost the product. Each of those feels true in the moment. On the right is what it really costs. It's never one prompt. It's many rounds, and every round burns tokens and someone's review time. Every design change made in code is another rebuild. And demos skip real data, so they get rebuilt for production anyway. Next: "Let's look at the two biggest costs."

X-Factory — Why change

06 / 18

(1:00) [Pause on the picture for a second.] Problem one. When the design only lives in the code, every piece of feedback means a rewrite. Try one. Someone looks at it: not quite. The agent rewrites it. Try two: not quite. Again. The red lines are the code that changed, and each try touches more of it, so things that worked before can break. Every round costs tokens, plus someone's time to review a brand-new diff. That's the bar at the bottom, and it only goes up. It rarely stops at four. One prompt at a time it feels fast. Added up, it's the most expensive place to iterate. Tip: if you have a real story from your team, a feature that took a dozen rounds, tell it here. Next: "And even when it finally looks right, there's a second problem."

X-Factory — Why change

07 / 18

(1:00) [Pause on the iceberg for a second.] Problem two. An AI-built demo can look finished on day one. It clicks through, it looks right, everyone's impressed. But what's actually done is the happy path, on sample data. That's the tip above the water. Underneath is everything a real product at Deriv needs. Real data and APIs. Every state: loading, empty, error. Every screen size. Our design system. Compliance copy and risk warnings, because we're regulated. Security. Tests. And a proper release. That's the part that takes the time. So the prototype gets rebuilt for production, and we pay for the same feature twice. Next: "So what do we do differently?"

X-Factory — Our answer

09 / 18

(1:00) Two moves, one for each problem. One: iterate the design, not the code. Every round of feedback happens on a mockup built from our real APIs and our real design system. Changing a mockup takes minutes and a few tokens, not a rebuild. That solves problem one. Two: ship the MVP first. One core flow, end to end, live on real data. Not a demo: a small product that actually works in production. Every feature after it lands on something that already works. That solves problem two. Next: "Which gives us three results."

More accurate.

X-Factory — The process

11 / 18

(1:00) Let's talk about how it actually runs. The top row is people, the bottom row is AI agents. You write your idea in idea.md, and /define-mvp turns it into mvp.md, which you approve. Then /feature-mockup draws the mockup, and you go back and forth until you approve it. From there you're hands off: /build-from-mockup builds and tests it, AI reviews it, our AI Release Manager ships it, and our Maintenance Agent looks after it. Planning happens once. Design, build and ship repeat, first for the MVP, then for every feature. Three commands, two approvals. Next: "Let's go through the five stages."

X-Factory — The process

12 / 18

(0:45) Stage one: plan. You write your idea in idea.md, in any shape. Then you run /define-mvp. The agent finds the one core flow the product can't live without, checks the real APIs so every step has real data behind it, and puts everything else into an ordered backlog. It writes all of that into mvp.md, with done-when checks we can test on the running app. You ask for changes until it's right, then approve it. This happens once per product.

X-Factory — The process

13 / 18

(0:45) Stage two: design, and this is where we iterate. We start with the MVP, then one feature at a time. /feature-mockup reads the real APIs and our design system, then writes two files: a markdown spec and an HTML mockup with desktop and mobile frames. You give feedback, and it updates the same two files. Each round takes minutes, not a rebuild. If data we need doesn't exist, it becomes an open question, never invented data. When you approve it, the mockup becomes the spec.

X-Factory — The process

14 / 18

(0:30) Stage three: build and test, in one step. /build-from-mockup only starts from an approved mockup. It writes a build plan, then AI subagents build the feature, write and run the tests, and check every screen against the mockup, on real data, desktop and mobile. It comes back with the evidence: test results and screenshots. No evidence, no review.

(0:30) Stage four: review and ship, already fully automated. Our AI review workflow in GitHub checks every pull request for bugs, security and compliance, and nothing merges without passing CI. Thank you. I'm happy to take questions about the process, the agents, or anything you saw in the workshop. Q&A prep, if it comes up: More time on design? Each round costs minutes and a few tokens instead of a rebuild, and the code is written once. Point back to "Build is no longer the constraint". Existing products? That path is next: each change goes through /feature-mockup and /build-from-mockup, and the agent reads the existing code, design system and APIs first. Who's accountable if AI reviews and releases? People approve mvp.md and every mockup. The agent that wrote the code never approves it, nothing merges without review and CI, and the service owner triages production. Does the agent make things up? It reads the real APIs first, gaps become open questions, and nothing goes to review without test results and screenshots. Numbers? We measure each team against its own baseline: time to approved spec, first-pass merge rate, rework, lead time to production, change failure rate. Share real figures only.
